extracted.intended_audience: authors, peer reviewers, and editors of observational epidemiology studies (manuscript authors preparing reports)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and reporting observational (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) epidemiologic studies so readers can judge validity, causality, applicability, and potential biases. Intended to inform manuscript preparation, peer review, and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of results — biases, confounding, and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting results, authors should consider the nature of the study on the discovery to verification continuum and potential sources of bias, including loss to follow-up and non-participation (see also items 9, 12 and 19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give due consideration to confounding (item 16a), the results of relevant sensitivity analyses, and to the issue of multiplicity and subgroup analyses (item 17). Consider residual confounding due to unmeasured variables or imprecise measurement of confounders (example: socioeconomic status variables are surrogates and measured with error). Authors should address the real range of uncertainty in estimates, which is larger than the statistical uncertainty reflected in confidence intervals, because CIs do not take into account uncertainties from study design, implementation, and measurement methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality considerations — use Bradford Hill criteria cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: To guide thinking and conclusions about causality, some may find criteria proposed by Bradford Hill in 1965 helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider strength of association, temporality (did exposure precede disease), consistency across studies/settings, supporting experimental evidence (including laboratory and animal studies), specificity, dose–response relationship, and biological plausibility. Do not apply these criteria mechanically: e.g., small relative risks (below 2 or 3) are not necessarily spurious, nor does a large RR automatically imply causality. Include discussion of existing external evidence from different study types, especially for small increases in risk, and put results in context with similar studies — ideally referring to a systematic review. Examples are provided (childhood leukaemia after intrauterine irradiation; dietary associations; enhancement of credibility by randomized cross-over trial findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability (external validity, applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the generalisability (external validity) of the study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalisability is meaningful only with clearly specified conditions. Ask whether results apply to individuals, groups or populations that differ by age, sex, ethnicity, disease severity, co-morbidity, exposure levels, and outcome definitions. Consider whether data collected long ago remain relevant and whether results from one country's health services apply to other health systems. Provide adequate information about setting and locations, eligibility criteria, the exposures and how they were measured, the definition of outcomes, and the period of recruitment and follow-up. Report degree of non-participation and the proportion of unexposed participants in whom the outcome develops. Knowledge of absolute risk and exposure prevalence, which often vary across populations, aids applying results to other settings (see Box 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualise results with external evidence and systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: A discussion of the existing external evidence, from different types of studies, should always be included, but may be particularly important for studies reporting small increases in risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should put their results in context with similar studies and explain how the new study affects the existing body of evidence, ideally by referring to a systematic review. Use evidence from other designs (e.g., experimental, lab, animal) where relevant to strengthen or question causal interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding disclosure and role of funders; conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the source of funding and the role of the funders for the present study and, if applicable, for the original study on which the present article is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose presence or absence of financial and other conflicts of interest. Recognise that funding source is often associated with study conclusions; funders or authors may influence design, choice of exposures, outcomes, statistical methods, and selective publication of outcomes and studies. Describe in detail the funders' role (e.g., design, data collection, analysis, drafting of manuscript, decision to publish). Also consider other sources of undue influence including employers, advisory committees, litigants, and special interest groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent and complete reporting; use and evolution of STROBE
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reporting reveals the strengths and weaknesses of a study and facilitates sound interpretation and application of study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: STROBE aims to assist authors and editors in transparent and complete reporting, may aid planning studies, and guide peer reviewers and editors in evaluation. Recognise that STROBE and other reporting recommendations should be seen as evolving documents that require continual assessment and refinement; authors and journals are invited to adopt and follow the STROBE Statement (see strobe-statement.org for discussion and updates).
